title: Erik Prince Pitched Contractor Plan for El Salvador Detention Camp
description_short: Erik Prince Pitched Contractor Plan for El Salvador Detention Camp
description_medium: Politico reported on April 11, 2025, that Erik Prince pitched the administration a plan for a 10,000-person detention camp and deportations of up to 100,000 people to El Salvador. The report said White House interest was unclear. It described a contractor proposal, not an approved $100 million contract or an operating deportation program.
description_long: Politico reported that Erik Prince pitched the administration a contractor plan involving a detention camp in El Salvador and possible deportations of up to 100,000 people. The supplied account described a proposed camp sized for 10,000 people and said White House interest was unclear. It does not establish an accepted proposal, a signed $100 million agreement, an operating camp, or deportations under the plan. The distinction matters: a private contractor’s pitch is not an administration decision or an implemented program. This description is limited to the proposal and its reported scale. subcategory: Foreign Prison Deportation Through Military Contractors

preserved_fields.title: El Salvador Prison Deportation - Erik Prince $100 Million Military Contractor Plan
preserved_fields.description_short: El Salvador Prison Deportation - Erik Prince $100 Million Military Contractor Plan
preserved_fields.description_long: Donald Trump's administration negotiated with former Blackwater CEO Erik Prince to implement an 'unprecedented prison plan' that would deport '100,000 of the worst criminal offenders' to El Salvador prisons through a $100 million military contractor operation involving 10,000-person detention camps and private aircraft fleets operated by Prince's defense contracting network. The systematic foreign deportation represented Trump's implementation of the most extreme immigration enforcement proposal in American history, using military contractors to transport detained immigrants from U.S. prisons to foreign detention facilities while Prince's company handled logistics for gathering prisoners, processing immigration files, and operating international detention operations. The El Salvador prison plan violated international law and constitutional due process protections by sending U.S. residents to foreign prisons without judicial review, while creating unprecedented privatization of immigration enforcement through military contractors who had previously operated in war zones using violence and weapons against civilian populations. Prince's deportation proposal demonstrated Trump's willingness to outsource core government functions to private military contractors while creating profit opportunities for defense industry allies who saw 'potential profits in mass deportations' through government contracts worth hundreds of millions of dollars. The foreign prison deportation violated sovereignty principles and international human rights law by using military contractors to forcibly transfer detainees to foreign countries without legal protections, judicial oversight, or diplomatic agreements ensuring humane treatment and legal representation for transported individuals. The unprecedented privatization represented what immigration advocates called 'extraordinary militarization' of deportation policy that treated immigration enforcement as military operation requiring private contractors with combat experience rather than law enforcement professionals trained in civil rights protections and due process procedures.

notes: The linked Politico page returned HTTP 403 during a focused read. The supplied account supports a reported contractor pitch, a proposed 10,000-person camp and possible deportations affecting up to 100,000 people; White House interest was unclear. No agreement, contract value, implementation, or actual deportation is established.

title: Trump Suspends Refugee Admissions Pending Review
description_short: Trump Suspends Refugee Admissions Pending Review
description_medium: Trump’s January 2025 order suspended entry under the U.S. Refugee Admissions Program starting January 27, pending a review of whether the program should resume. It also paused decisions on refugee applications, while allowing case-by-case admissions when officials found entry to be in the national interest. The order called for an initial report within 90 days and further reports every 90 days.
description_long: The January 2025 order suspended entry under the U.S. Refugee Admissions Program beginning January 27 while the administration reviewed whether admissions should resume. It also paused decisions on refugee applications during the review. The order allowed case-by-case admissions when officials determined that an exception served the national interest, and it required an initial report within 90 days followed by recurring 90-day reports. These terms describe a suspension and review process, not a permanent termination of refugee admissions. The supplied order does not establish the preserved long description’s separate claims that asylum, Temporary Protected Status, T and U visas, or immigration agencies were eliminated or consolidated. Those claims are removed from this account; the record does not state the outcome of the review.

preserved_fields.title: Refugee Admissions and Asylum Elimination - Complete Protection System Termination
preserved_fields.description_short: Refugee Admissions and Asylum Elimination - Complete Protection System Termination
preserved_fields.description_long: Donald Trump terminated the United States Refugee Admissions Program and eliminated asylum pathways by suspending all refugee processing, ending Temporary Protected Status for 850,000 individuals, and eliminating T and U visas for victims of human trafficking and violent crimes while consolidating immigration agencies into single enforcement entity without humanitarian functions. The comprehensive protection elimination represented Trump's implementation of Project 2025's plan to 'slash immigration levels' by removing all pathways for vulnerable individuals to seek safety in the United States, effectively ending America's historic role as refuge for people fleeing persecution, violence, and humanitarian disasters. The systematic asylum destruction included directing USCIS to cease application intake for asylum, TPS, and victim visas whenever backlogs were deemed 'excessive,' creating deliberate administrative barriers that prevented eligible individuals from accessing legal protections while forcing them into undocumented status vulnerable to deportation. Trump's refugee program termination violated international humanitarian law obligations by ending protections for individuals fleeing 'armed conflicts or environmental disasters' while eliminating work authorization that had allowed protected individuals to rebuild lives and contribute economically to American communities. The protection system elimination consolidated key immigration agencies into single powerful entity that 'stripped oversight and accountability from ICE' while removing humanitarian considerations from immigration decisions, transforming what had been 'fair immigration system into one driven by enforcement and exclusion' rather than protection of vulnerable populations. The refugee and asylum termination represented what human rights organizations called abandonment of American values and international obligations, ending decades of humanitarian leadership while forcing vulnerable individuals back to countries where they faced persecution, violence, or death due to conditions beyond their control.

title: Evercore Acquires American Media; David Pecker Becomes CEO

description_long: On February 17, 1999, Evercore Partners acquired American Media Inc., the publisher of the National Enquirer and Star. Evercore was led by Roger Altman, and David Pecker, then an executive at Hachette Filipacchi, was hired to lead American Media as chairman and chief executive. The transaction changed control of the parent publisher and put Pecker in charge of its publications; it was not a personal purchase of the Enquirer by Pecker. The distinction matters because the title describes a different buyer and a separate claim about the paper’s earlier history. This transaction record does not establish whether the National Enquirer had previously received Mafia financing, and the 1999 acquisition itself is not reported as involving Donald Trump. Pecker’s later relationship with Trump should not be projected backward onto the purchase. The reported event is Evercore’s acquisition of American Media and Pecker’s appointment to run the company.
